rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The White Horse
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a snowy white horse with a silver mane stepping out from between pale stone statues in a moonlit garden, a girl in a white dress riding bareback while three children walk beside her with a lantern, yew hedges and a sleeping castle beyond, full moon and silver light, dreamy storybook illustration

blocks.text: The princess game needed more than a garden to play in. A true princess must ride to her enchanted castle, and there was no horse to be had anywhere. "Then we shall wish for one," said Gerald. He held the ring tight and wished - out loud, as they had learned to do. Nobody quite believed that anything would happen.
The white horse comes at a wish - and it is made of moonlight and chalk.

And the horse came. It stepped out from behind the statues, snow-white and shining, with a mane like sea-spray. But when Jimmy touched it, it felt strange. Not warm like a pony, but hard and thin, like chalk and moonlight pressed together. Mabel climbed up all the same, and they led her round the garden. The statues bowed low as she passed.
Talk together: The horse was made from the garden's own stone and light. Why might magic that borrows real things have to give them back?

They rode and walked and led the horse until the moon went down behind the yew trees. At dawn the white horse stood still in the wet grass. Then, gently, it came apart - a soft hill of dust, a shimmer, and nothing but the green lawn. The children stared at the empty air. "The ring made a horse out of the garden itself," said Kathleen slowly. "Wishes are big things," said Gerald. "We have been playing with them like toys."

That day they were careful, or tried to be. But the ring lay warm in Mabel's pocket, and warm things want using. The princess game was not over yet either. A sleeping princess, a castle, and now a horse come and gone - the game grew truer every day. And with it, without meaning to, they began to plan something much bigger. They did not know yet how big.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · Breakfast in Town
chapters.artPrompt: a grand dining room of an old inn where silver teapots and plates of eggs and toast float in mid-air above an empty chair, waiters frozen in fright with dropped napkins, a girl laughing behind her menu, a head waiter staring at a printed bill, bright morning light through tall windows, funny gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: Kathleen had been thinking, and thinking is dangerous when there is a wishing ring in the house. "If the ring can make a horse," she said, "it can make us ladies for a morning." So Mabel slipped on the ring and vanished. Kathleen walked beside the empty air, talking to her all the way to town. The morning was bright, and the town lay only three fields away.
An invisible girl orders a grand breakfast, and the spoons move by themselves.

At the Rose and Crown they ordered everything: eggs and bacon, honey, hot buttered toast, and chocolate. The waiters watched one girl eat for two, and watched a second plate empty itself in the air. They fled, crying that the inn was haunted. The girls laughed till their sides ached. Then the bill came, written out in neat black figures. The head waiter laid it down softly, and tiptoed away. And invisible ladies, it turned out, have no purses at all.
Talk together: The children make one wish for fun and one wish for help. When does a game begin to cost something?

"Pay it!" whispered Mabel, and the ring obeyed. Gold coins rang out on the cloth. But at home that evening Mabel's aunt unlocked her savings-box and found it light. The ring had not made money. It had only moved it - out of a kind old lady's tin box. The girls went very quiet, and then very red.

"We took what was not ours," said Kathleen, "even if the ring did the taking." They could not confess without telling everything about the ring. So they began, very seriously, to plan how to fill that savings-box again - honestly, with money of their own. Ninepence of pocket-money was not going to do it. And out of that plan came the grandest idea of the whole summer.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Burglar
chapters.artPrompt: inside a dark castle hall at night, a startled thief in a black jersey holding a small shaded lantern before an open treasure cupboard of golden cups, a polite empty patch of shadow speaking beside him, one tall window with deep blue moonlight, tense but gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: One dark night a real burglar came to the castle. The moon was hidden, and the night smelled of rain. He had soft boots, a black jersey, and a little dark lantern, and he knew that old houses keep gold. He found the little door, and the treasure room, and the shelves where the gold cups stood in rows. And in the corner, quite invisible, stood Gerald, with the ring on his finger.
The treasure room is full of gold - and one boy nobody can see.

"Good evening," said a polite voice out of the empty air. "I am afraid you have chosen the wrong castle." The lantern shook in the thief's hand. The voice gave him friendly directions: which stair creaked, which window stuck, and how far away the constable lived. The burglar set down the candlestick he had pocketed, backed to the window, and ran for his life.
New word: burglar - a thief who creeps into houses at night. This one was beaten by a boy he never saw at all.

In the morning the town was full of the story. A gentleman in the castle, people said, had spoken kindly to the thief and frightened him out of his wits. Only the dropped candlestick told of a thief at all. "A ghost that is on our side," said Mabel's aunt, looking pleased. The children looked at one another and said nothing at all.

But Gerald's head was full of something else. Mabel's aunt was helping at the church bazaar, and the bazaar wanted a marvel to draw the crowd. "A castle with a friendly ghost," said Gerald slowly, "could sell a great many tickets." "Only we shall have to be careful what we wish for," said Jimmy. Nobody guessed yet how careful. And so the plan of the bazaar play was born.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Wonderful Play
chapters.artPrompt: a candlelit great hall in an old castle where children in borrowed velvet perform a play of a sleeping princess in a paper rose tower, a crowd of townsfolk applauding in rows of chairs, gold chairs and velvet curtains glowing, warm golden light and deep shadows, festive storybook illustration

blocks.text: The bazaar was fixed for midsummer, and the children promised the aunt a play that would fill the castle hall. They would act the very tale that had begun it all. It was the tale of the thirteenth princess, asleep a hundred years in her tower. Rehearsals were held in secret, with the door of the tapestry room shut. Jimmy painted the enchanted moon on a bedsheet, and it was very good indeed. The aunt sighed over her savings-box, then lent them the hall, the velvet curtains, and the old gold chairs.
The children act the sleeping princess, and the whole town comes to see.

Gerald, wrapped in a borrowed cloak, played the invisible gentleman. For that one scene he did not need to act at all. Mabel slept like a truly enchanted princess. The ring, worn secretly under a glove, made the paper roses glitter. The little stage shone brighter than the lamps had any right to shine. The townsfolk came in their Sunday best and clapped until their hands were sore.
Question for you: The play tells the true story of the ring, and nobody in the seats knows it. Why is it fun to hide a true secret inside a pretend one?

The play earned a great deal of money. The first coins of it went, quietly, into a certain tin savings-box, a few at a time. The aunt never guessed why her bazaar took more money than anyone could remember. She only said the castle had luck in it again, and let the children keep the keys of the hall.

That night the ring lay in the treasure room, warm and humming, like a kettle not quite done boiling. "It is not tired at all," whispered Mabel. "It is only just beginning." And she was right, though none of them knew yet what was beginning, or how very large it would be.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Ugly-Wuglies' Second Act
chapters.artPrompt: a row of wobbly paper gentlemen in old coats and straw hats coming to life on a castle terrace at dusk, one neat paper gentleman in a bowler hat bowing politely before four astonished children, long evening shadows across a moonlit lawn, funny gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: After the play, when the hall was dark and the town was abed, the paper people stirred. The ring had lain near them once more, and the ring was not tired. The children found them walking on the moonlit terrace, solid grown-ups now, in old coats and straw hats. They looked very pleased with themselves. "A most respectable entertainment," said the fat one. They shook hands with the children, one by one, in a wobbly, papery way.
The paper gentlemen bow, thank their hosts, and ask the way to the station.

The Ugly-Wuglies wished to see the world. At moonset most of them folded softly down into flat paper again, smiling their crayon smiles. But the neat one in the bowler hat had already started down the road. He was walking toward the town and the morning train. "I have an appointment," he said, "in the City." And he kept it.
New word: the City - the busy business heart of a great town, full of banks and offices. One paper gentleman went there to seek his fortune.

Weeks later the children heard of a new gentleman in the town. He was quiet, neat, and wonderful at figures, and rising fast in the world. He wore gloves all the time and never spoke of his boyhood. Shopkeepers liked him, and the bank liked him. He was said to be saving up for a little house in the country. Only four children in England knew where his smile had first been drawn, and with what.

"We cannot un-wish him," said Mabel. "Nor do I want to," said Gerald, "if he does no harm." So they let the paper gentleman alone, and he went on doing well. He was the politest, and the strangest, of all the works of the ring. And to this day, people say, his business does wonderfully well.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Other Rings
chapters.artPrompt: an open green velvet case in a dim treasure room holding many small glowing rings of different shapes, four children bending close with a candle, one ring lifted high shining like a tiny moon, gold cups faint in the shadows behind, mysterious warm light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The ring kept a secret, and Mabel found it. Behind a loose shelf in the treasure room lay a little case lined with green velvet. The case held other rings, small and bright - cousins of theirs. They shone like tiny moons in the dark. The children looked at them with round eyes. More rings meant more magic, and more magic, they thought, meant more of everything.
The velvet case holds more wishing rings than the children ever dreamed of.

But the rings came with no instructions at all. Each one answered to a different kind of wish, and nobody remembered which was which. A wish made in fun tangled with a wish made in fear. Soon the garden was full of small magics tumbling over one another. There was a fountain that rained upward, and statues bowing to the wrong people. Kathleen's hat was wished onto a yew tree at the far side of the park.
Talk together: The children thought more rings would mean more fun. Why can too much of a wonderful thing turn into a muddle?

It took a whole moonlit evening to say good-bye to every wish. One by one, the rings were laid quietly back in their case. Even the one that had rained the fountain upward went still and quiet. "The ring is not a toy box," said Kathleen at last. "It is a door." And a door, they were beginning to understand, opens both ways.

That night the garden seemed to be listening harder than usual. The statues stood very straight, and the moon rose larger and whiter than they had ever seen it. The four friends went out after supper, without saying why. Something was going to happen soon. The garden itself, they felt sure, was going to show them what the rings had really been for.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The House of the Temples
chapters.artPrompt: two children walking hand in hand through a long ruined colonnade of pale stone arches glowing under a full moon, a silver garden of drifting statues opening beyond, a huge gentle dinosaur-shaped shadow grazing far away among trees, deep blue and silver light, dreamlike storybook illustration

blocks.text: At the next full moon, Gerald and Mabel did what the statues did. Beyond the last yew hedge they found a colonnade nobody had ever seen by day. It was a long walk of pale arches, standing in silver light. The stones underfoot were pale as bone and smooth as shells. The old garden stories called it the house of the temples. Hand in hand, the two of them walked through.
Beyond the arches, the moon-country opens like a garden of dreams.

The country beyond was the place the magic came from. Statues walked there in the silver grass, and wishes were born there, and everything was beautiful and a little sad. It was like music heard from a room away. Nobody here was surprised to see children. The statues bowed, as if they had been expected for a hundred years. Far off among the trees a great gentle beast grazed, nodding slowly as it cropped the leaves. The children understood, without being told, that this was not a place to stay.
New word: colonnade - a roofed walk lined with pillars. Old gardens sometimes keep such walks, cool and quiet in the heat of the day.

"All our wishes walked out from here," whispered Mabel. Gerald looked at the arches, at the bowing statues, at the sleeping castle far behind. "Then the ring belongs here," he said, "not in a pocket." The moonlight ran along the stones, like a slow and kindly nod. And somewhere far off, the great beast lifted its head.

They did not say good-bye yet. First they must go home and tell the others, and pack the holiday trunks, and be brave about it. But both of them knew what the last night of the summer was going to be for. Behind them, softly, the arches shone like a row of little moons.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Ring Goes Home
chapters.artPrompt: two children placing a small glowing silver ring on a low pale stone altar covered in white moonflowers, stone statues bowing in a circle around them, a huge gentle beast watching from among moonlit trees, the castle small and dark far behind, silver and gold light, gentle bittersweet storybook illustration

blocks.text: On the last night of the holidays, the four friends carried the ring through the house of the temples. Out in the silver country beyond, Gerald set it down gently, just where the moonlight began. The moon was at its full and brightest, and not a cloud was anywhere. The statues drew near and bowed. Somewhere far off, the great gentle beast lifted its head, as if to say thank you.
The ring is laid down where the moonlight begins, and the garden says good-bye.

"It was never ours," said Mabel. "Only lent." The ring glowed once, warmly, like a hand squeezed in farewell. Then it grew quiet among the white flowers. The moonflowers closed their petals softly, one by one. When the children turned round, the colonnade was old stones again. The garden was only a garden in the dark. But not everything went back.
Talk together: The children give the ring back and keep everything they learned. Why does saying good-bye not spoil the wonderful part?

The neat gentleman in the bowler hat stayed real. He went on prospering in the City, doing wonderfully well at figures. Nobody ever learned his name, and nobody ever needed to. "Some wishes grow roots," said Gerald. "He was wished so hard, and so kindly, that the world has decided to keep him."

Next morning the castle was only a grand old house again. Mabel's aunt wondered why the children smiled at breakfast for no reason at all. They packed their trunks and caught the morning train. And the four friends knew they would come back one day, just to look over the wall. But each of them carried away a summer that held a castle, a moon, and a secret. It was a secret that would never wear out.
